Zimmie Reva Shelton
Spelman College graduate, class of 1929; Atlanta art teacher.

Her Spelman education supported a long teaching career.
In 2022 Spelman dedicated its admissions office to Shelton and her daughter, Jacquelyn Shelton Lee.

Shelton taught art in Atlanta public schools for approximately fifty years. She was the maternal grandmother of filmmaker Shelton Jackson "Spike" Lee.
She saved Social Security payments for her grandchildren's education, helping Lee attend Morehouse College and New York University, and supplied early funding for She's Gotta Have It.
She married postal employee Richard Jackson Shelton, who died in 1976.

Jewel Woodward Simon
Atlanta University graduate, summa cum laude; artist and mathematics teacher.

Her Atlanta University education preceded a career in painting, sculpture and printmaking.
She helped found the National Conference of Negro Artists and participated in civic arts leadership.

Born in Houston, Simon combined interests in mathematics, visual arts, music and poetry. She taught mathematics at Jack Yates High School before settling in Atlanta with her husband Edward Lloyd Simon.
She studied painting with Hale Woodruff and sculpture with Alice Dunbar and became the first Black graduate awarded a BFA by the Atlanta School of Art in 1967.

Louie Delphia Davis Shivery
Atlanta University master's graduate; educator and social-welfare historian.

Her Atlanta University research documented organized social work among Black Atlantans from 1890 to 1935.
She helped develop the Neighborhood Union and served as its executive secretary and historian.

Shivery headed the English department at Booker T. Washington High School and wrote its school song.
She contributed to the Atlanta Daily World and held leadership roles in Black women's civic organizations, including the Atlanta Metropolitan Council of Negro Women. She also served the Colored Branch of the Atlanta Tuberculosis Association.

Clark Atlanta University
Nellie Harriet Watts
Atlanta University graduate; Detroit educator and concert promoter.
Her Nellie Watts Concert Series expanded opportunities for Black performing artists for twenty-five years.

Watts also graduated from Detroit Teachers College and taught in Detroit public schools. In 1937 she financed Marian Anderson's first Detroit performance.
Her concert series presented artists including Leontyne Price, Paul Robeson and the Alvin Ailey Dance Theatre. She founded an arts-support organization and served on the Detroit NAACP board.
She was a daughter of South-View co-founder Albert Watts.

Clark Atlanta University
Wilmere Kathleen Redding Adams
Completed Atlanta University's high school and normal teacher-training course in 1911.

Applied her Atlanta University training in public education and service to children.
Preserved the history of Auburn Avenue and Black education in Atlanta.

Adams grew up on Auburn Avenue, the daughter of Wesley Chapel Redding and Ellen Redding.
She taught in Atlanta and Fulton County schools and at the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home. She preserved local history through oral histories and her service as historian of First Congregational Church. The book also records her Auburn Avenue Research Library board service.

Julia Agnes Washington Bond
Atlanta University library-science master's graduate and librarian; retired in 2000.
Sustained the Atlanta University Center's scholarly community through decades of library service.

Bond was born in Nashville and attended Fisk University, where she met educator Horace Mann Bond.
She returned to school at age fifty-six to study library science at Atlanta University. She worked at Trevor Arnett Library and later as a part-time reference librarian at Robert W. Woodruff Library.
She and her husband supported their children's civil rights work, including Julian Bond's. She retired in 2000 at ninety-two.

Minnie Dyer
Graduate of Morris Brown College and Atlanta University; Atlanta elementary-school teacher.
Put her college education into practice in Atlanta schools during segregation, supporting generations of elementary-school students.

Dyer was a daughter of Caleb and Emma Dyer. Her father, a carpenter, purchased the family's first cemetery land at South-View.
She worked as a seamstress before earning teaching credentials. After temporary teaching work in 1910, she joined Mitchell Street School full time in 1911. She later taught at Ashby Street School and Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic School.
Her niece and pupil, Pearlie Craft Dove, became a noted educator at Clark College.

Harold Irvin Bearden
Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary graduate; later chaired Morris Brown's trustees.

Helped Morris Brown work toward accreditation as chair of its trustees.
Combined educational leadership with AME ministry and advocacy against segregation.

Bearden became pastor of Big Bethel AME Church in Atlanta in 1951. His radio sermons reached a wide audience, and he participated in civil rights protests.
He served as president of the Atlanta NAACP and was elected an AME bishop in 1964.

Fred C. Bennette Jr.
Morris Brown and Turner Theological Seminary alumnus; student civil rights organizer.

Organized against segregation at Rich's department store while a Morris Brown student.
Became the first director of SCLC's Operation Breadbasket.

Bennette served in the U.S. Army before returning to Atlanta for further education and civil rights work.
He organized voter-registration campaigns and worked closely with Martin Luther King Jr. and Andrew Young. He later advised Jimmy Carter and Young and served the King Center as an adviser and security director.

Morris Brown College
Hilliard D. Canady
Attended Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary; AME presiding elder.
His Morris Brown and Turner education supported his career in African Methodist Episcopal ministry.

Canady was born in Troup County, Georgia, in 1859 and also attended Meharry Medical College. He served as a presiding elder in the AME Church.
His wife, Nora Lee Bryant Canady, was a Clark College graduate and church worker. Their son, Hilliard D. Canady Jr., became a physician and medical inspector of Atlanta's Black public schools. Father and son died in 1932.

William Alfred Fountain Sr.
Morris Brown alumnus and fifth president, 1911–1920; later chancellor.

Led Morris Brown as president and later chancellor.
Fountain Hall bears his name and connects Morris Brown with the former Atlanta University campus.

Fountain was an AME minister who became a bishop in 1920. He held degrees from Morris Brown and Turner Theological Seminary and pursued further education elsewhere.
He strengthened congregations, participated in civic organizations and worked to sustain Black higher education alongside his son William Alfred Fountain Jr.

Morris Brown College
William Alfred Fountain Jr.
Seventh president of Morris Brown College, serving 1929–1950.

Helped keep Morris Brown operating through the Great Depression.
During his administration the college joined the Atlanta University Center and relocated to the former Atlanta University campus.

Fountain Jr. led Morris Brown during severe financial hardship. The book describes his decision to forgo salary while the institution reorganized. His father, a former president, served as chancellor during the early years of his administration.
After his presidency he served as secretary-treasurer of the AME Church's General Board of Education.

Evelyn Jones Frazier
Morris Brown College graduate, 1952; Atlanta restaurant owner and civic leader.

Earned her Morris Brown bachelor's degree in 1952 while developing her restaurant business.
Her restaurant provided meeting space for Black civic, religious and civil rights organizations.

Frazier opened the Evelyn Jones Cafe in 1936 and expanded it with her husband Luther Ellis Frazier in the 1940s as Frazier's Cafe Society.
The restaurant became a gathering place for leaders including Benjamin Mays, Martin Luther King Jr. and Thurgood Marshall. She supported businesswomen's organizations and the NAACP. Her funeral notice confirms interment at South-View.

Cornelius King
Trustee of Morris Brown College; real-estate entrepreneur and hospital organizer.

Served Morris Brown as trustee and Big Bethel AME Church as trustee-board chair.
Helped organize Mercy Hospital in 1919 and served as superintendent.

King worked in Atlanta's private clubs and later in Washington, D.C., before developing businesses that served Black Atlantans.
He opened King's Wigwam, a recreation resort near Kennesaw, in 1918 and founded Cornelius King & Son real estate in 1922. His second wife Nina Culver King was a Spelman graduate. His son Turner later headed the family firm.

John Henry Lewis
Morris Brown graduate, 1905; sixth and eighth president, 1920–1928 and 1951–1958.

Taught at Morris Brown and led it through two presidencies.
His wider educational leadership included Dunbar High School, Shorter College and Payne Theological Seminary.

Born in Ellaville, Georgia, Lewis studied ministry at Yale Divinity School and pursued graduate education at the University of Chicago.
He served as an AME minister and educational administrator in several states before returning to Morris Brown for his second presidency, which continued until his death. Historian David Levering Lewis was his son.

Morris Brown College
John Wesley Edward Linder
Morris Brown College graduate; physician and medical-association leader.
His education and professional leadership supported Black physicians and patients in segregated Georgia.

Linder continued to Meharry Medical College and initially practiced medicine in Dublin, Georgia, before relocating to Atlanta.
He served as president of the Atlanta and Georgia medical associations and began the Georgia association's first quarterly journal. He also served on the National Medical Association's executive board.

Morehouse College
Henry James Charles Bowden
Morehouse College graduate, class of 1925; Episcopal priest and advocate for older adults.

Connected ministry with service and advocacy for older adults.
Fulton County's H.J.C. Bowden senior multipurpose facility recognizes his work.

Bowden continued at General Theological Seminary and Columbia University. Ordained in 1929, he became rector of St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Atlanta in 1934.
He served as a military and Veterans Administration chaplain and worked with aging-service organizations and the NAACP.

Morehouse College
Clifford Nathaniel Ellis
Morehouse graduate, 1926; Morehouse School of Religion graduate, 1927.

Applied Morehouse training in a long pastoral career.
Extended the church's reach through Chariot Wheels gospel broadcasting and national Baptist leadership.

Born in Chattanooga, Ellis completed Morehouse Academy before his college and divinity degrees. He pastored Georgia churches and led Reed Street, later Paradise, Baptist Church for more than four decades.
He served as president of the Atlanta Baptist Ministers Union. His wife Vashti Scott Ellis was a journalist in the Atlanta Daily World publishing family.

Morehouse College
Charles Walter Greenlea
Morehouse College graduate; Atlanta University master's graduate.

Applied his education to journalism, civil rights and community development.
Greenlea Commons in Summerhill was named in his honor.

Known as Pete, Greenlea served for twenty years as executive director of the Atlanta NAACP. He worked as an editor at the Atlanta Daily World and with Economic Opportunity Atlanta.
He co-founded and led Summerhill Neighborhood Inc., connecting community organizing with housing and neighborhood development.

Rogers Henderson
Honorary alumnus and supporter of Morehouse College; real-estate entrepreneur.
Morehouse honored him as an honorary alumnus, reflecting his support rather than an earned degree.

Henderson founded Henderson Realty Company on Auburn Avenue and helped establish the Empire Real Estate Board. His wife Ida Franklin Henderson joined the business and held leadership roles in Black women's civic organizations.
The couple supported Morehouse's Danforth Chapel with a stained-glass window and painting.

Charles Dubois Hubert
Morehouse graduate, 1909; religion-school director and acting president, 1937–1940.

Guided Morehouse as acting president between Samuel Archer and Benjamin Mays.
Combined scholarship with pastoral and educational leadership.

Hubert grew up in Hancock County, Georgia, and completed Morehouse Academy in 1905. He earned a Morehouse bachelor's degree in 1909 and a divinity degree from Rochester Theological Seminary in 1912.
He taught church history, directed Morehouse's School of Religion and served as pastor of Providence Baptist Church.

Morehouse College
Dennis Taylor Hubert
Morehouse divinity student in 1930; awarded a posthumous honorary degree in 2025.

His interrupted education is part of Morehouse's history.
Morehouse honored his life in its 2025 commencement with a posthumous honorary bachelor's degree.

Hubert was eighteen when a white mob killed him on the Crogman School playground in Atlanta on June 15, 1930.
He was a son of minister Gaddus Johnson Hubert and educator Pearl Parks Hubert and nephew of Charles Dubois Hubert. The killing and attacks against his family illustrate the racial terror that constrained Black life and education.

Morehouse College
Graham Washington Jackson
Attended Morehouse College and Atlanta University; musician and music educator.

Connected college study with music education and performance in Atlanta.
Jimmy Carter named him Georgia's official state musician.

Born in Portsmouth, Virginia, Jackson became known for piano, organ and accordion performance. He led music at Booker T. Washington High School and performed at wartime fundraising events and for U.S. presidents.
A widely circulated 1945 photograph shows him playing accordion in mourning for Franklin Roosevelt. His career also included jazz-band leadership, broadcasting and public performances.

Phoebe Lucille Fraser Burney Callier Hart
Clark College graduate, 1935; dean of women, 1943–1958.

Guided Clark students for fifteen years as dean of women.
Connected religious education with administration at several Black colleges.

Hart pursued religious-education study at Gammon Theological Seminary after her Clark degree. She directed Congregational religious education and worked in Morehouse's endowment office before becoming Clark's dean of women.
Later known as Phoebe Callier, she served educational institutions in Chattanooga. The book also records her sponsorship of two African students.

Spelman College
Cora B. Finley
Spelman graduate; first Spelman alumna to earn an advanced degree at Atlanta University, according to Henderson.
Applied Spelman and Atlanta University education in school leadership, adult education and advocacy for teachers.

Finley was principal of Atlanta's Yonge Street School. She helped organize an early Black parent-teacher association in 1911 and challenged unequal teacher salaries through the Gate City Teachers Association.
She worked with the NAACP, served on the first board of the Atlanta Urban League, organized a night school and later led Alabama State University's education department.

Spelman College
Estelle B. Ivey
Graduate of Spelman's historical nursing school; Ivey Brothers Funeral Home business officer.
Her Spelman training and business service connected the college with an important Black-owned funeral enterprise.

Ivey and her four brothers grew up in the Carrie Steele orphanage after their parents died. Henry and James established Ivey Brothers Funeral Home in 1912.
Estelle worked as bookkeeper, secretary and treasurer. The family enterprise supported churches, charitable work and families with limited financial means.

Spelman College
Clara Ivey Wilson
Spelman College graduate, class of 1938; funeral-home owner and South-View board leader.

Continued her family's funeral-service and civic leadership.
Spelman's Ivey-Wilson endowed scholarship commemorates her as a member of its class of 1938.

Wilson succeeded her father Henry M. Ivey in ownership and leadership of Ivey Brothers Funeral Home. She also followed him onto South-View's board and served as second vice president.
A 1962 Atlanta Daily World account records her service with Gate City Day Nurseries and Delta Sigma Theta and jury duty in Fulton County.

Nina Culver King
Spelman College graduate; member of Atlanta's King family of business and civic leaders.
Her Spelman education connects the college to the family of Morris Brown trustee and entrepreneur Cornelius King.

King worked in the United States Patent Office in Washington, D.C., where she met Cornelius King. She became his second wife.

Spelman College
Alberta Williams King
Spelman Seminary high school graduate, 1922; later Morris Brown College graduate.

Her historical Spelman Seminary education preceded teacher training at Hampton and a Morris Brown bachelor's degree in 1938.
Spelman's Alberta Williams King Memorial Endowed Scholarship connects her legacy with music and nonviolence studies.

King was the daughter of Ebenezer Baptist Church pastor Adam Daniel Williams and Jennie Celeste Williams. She led Ebenezer's choir and served for decades as organist and music director.
She raised her family with Martin Luther King Sr. and was the mother of Martin Luther King Jr. She was killed while playing the church organ in June 1974.

Spelman College
Flora Ethelwyn Zeto Malekebu
Spelman High School graduate, 1915; co-namesake of Gordon-Zeto Center for Global Education.

Spelman identifies Zeto as its first African graduate from the historical high school program in 1915.
Her education and missionary service form part of Spelman's international legacy.

As a child Flora Zeto came from the Congo to Atlanta with Spelman alumna and missionary Clara A. Howard.
She married physician Daniel Sharpe Malekebu, who had also come from Africa with a missionary and later trained at Meharry Medical College.
The couple worked in African missions and maintained U.S. connections. National Baptist Convention records identify Flora as an assistant at Providence Industrial Mission in Nyasaland.
